headline: Bestinet ran Malaysia's visa system: RM400M to founder's firms, no contract, Interpol arrest request
context: Bloomberg's 10-month investigation found Bestinet founder Aminul Islam's firms made over RM400M in 10 years. Workers pay up to RM25,000 in recruitment fees. MACC closed its probe in September 2024; Cabinet extended the contract to 2031.

changes.summary: Correction: Earlier editions overstated Zahid Hamidi's role in the 10-agency recruitment limit and the Bestinet founder's personal gain. The cards now say Zahid was Home Minister when the limit began and that six sources told Bloomberg he handled the politics, which he denies, and that the founder's firms made the RM400M. Visa-time and tender figures we could not confirm are removed.

Correction: we removed a handover deadline, a claim about who should pay permit fees and a reference to communities that we could not confirm; we now attribute the source-code claim to the politician who made it and give the company's reply, and state the RM400M figure, the contract, the fee comparison and the arrest request more precisely.

Correction: the reframe said Malaysian businesses profit from bonded labour while working-class Malaysians bear wage suppression, a causal claim no source supports. It now asks why the visa system ran for nearly six years without a contract, as Parliament's Public Accounts Committee found.

cards.big: One firm runs Malaysia's migrant visa system. Its founder faced an Interpol arrest request. The government extended its contract to 2031.
cards.sub: Bloomberg found his firms made over RM400M. Workers pay up to RM25,000. MACC closed its probe in Sept 2024, four months after Cabinet agreed the extension.

cards.big: Six years with no signed contract. Then the per-worker fee was set at RM215, more than double the government's own RM86 rate.
cards.sub: PAC found 24 unauthorised users approving employer applications. Rafizi Ramli says the government never got the source code; Bestinet says it hands it over at contract end.

cards.big: Bangladesh sought the founder's arrest via Interpol. Malaysia asked Bangladesh to drop its trafficking probes to protect its TIP ranking.
cards.sub: A 2023 ILO survey found 29% of migrant domestic workers in Malaysia in forced-labour conditions.

cards.big: Zahid was Home Minister in 2015, when Bangladeshi recruitment was cut to 10 agencies. Six sources told Bloomberg he handled the politics. He denies involvement.
cards.sub: Anwar's Cabinet agreed in May 2024 to extend the contract, after a memo prepared for him put recruitment costs at up to RM25,000 a worker.

cards.big: Why did Malaysia's migrant visa system run for nearly six years without a signed contract?
Like outsourcing passport control to a toll-booth operator who cut wait times, then learning it charges more than double the approved rate and ran six years without a contract.
cards.sub: Speed built on worker debt bondage is not efficiency. It is exploitation with a dashboard.

cards.big: The fix exists: open tendering, employer-pays enforcement, cooperation with Bangladesh. No coalition will accept the disruption.
